--- Page 5 ---
<meta>This is the title page of Jacob Böhme's third major work. It establishes the foundational themes of his mystical philosophy, specifically the "Three Principles" of divine manifestation.</meta>

# ON THE THREEFOLD LIFE OF MAN,
->or<-
### High and Deep Foundations
# Of the Threefold Life of Man.

---

### Brief Summary of this Book.

In this work, the Eternal as well as the Mortal is clearly shown; and why God, the highest Good, has brought all things to light; also why one thing runs against another and perishes; and then what is Right or False, and how one is separated from the other.

2. Within this are primarily established the three **Principles** <note>original: "Principia"; Böhme uses this term to describe the three fundamental realms of existence: the dark fire-world, the light-world, and the outer visible world.</note>, which are the single ground or fountain-spring from which all things flow and are born. From this is clearly recognized the various opinions of faith, why and for what reasons there are so many different opinions among men concerning the Divine Being and Will; also what is useful for man to do so that he may attain the highest Eternal Good.

3. And then concerning the departure and end of all things; why all things have appeared in such torment and in such a state. For the comfort of the poor, wounded, and sick soul of man, and for the edification of the true Christian religion; wherein the Antichrist <note>original: "Wiederchrist"; Böhme often used this term to refer to institutionalized "stone churches" that lacked spiritual life.</note> stands completely naked and revealed.

Composed for our own remembrance and encouragement in this confused and sorrowful time, in the year 1620.

<sig>A</sig>
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

<summary>The title page and introduction to Jacob Böhme's treatise on the "Threefold Life of Man," outlining his mystical cosmology and the origins of good and evil. It presents the work as a guide for the soul to find the "highest Good" amidst the religious confusion of the early 17th century.</summary>
<keywords>Threefold Life, Three Principles, Jacob Böhme, Mysticism, Divine Will, Antichrist, 1620, Cosmology, Spiritual Edification</keywords>

## The 1st Chapter.
# Concerning the Origin <note>original: "Urkund," referring to the primal source or original record</note> of Life: Likewise concerning the Eternal Birth of the Divine Being.
### Summaries.

We are not at home in the outward life. §. 1. Three kinds of life are manifest in us, 2. namely, the outward, which is a burning fire, 3. that of the soul, which is also a fire; and therein yet a greater hunger, which desires God for food: 4. 5. for as every life desires its mother for food. 6. The elemental life stands in the seething <note>original: "Sude," referring to the boiling or bubbling of natural forces</note>, 7. and the soul-life is eternal. 8. All 3 lives, however, stand within one another: and yet each has its own working in its own dominion <note>original: "Regiment"</note>, as in its mother. 9. The soul is infected by the stars, 10. but has another food, and lives in another Principle <note>term: "Principle" (Principium) - Böhme's term for the three distinct realms of existence: the dark fire-world, the light holy-world, and the outer visible world</note>; 11. its essences are from eternal nature, ibid. which is indeed also in God, yet so that God’s Spirit is not subject to it; 12. it hungers after God’s power: but cannot enter with its whole being into God’s power; 13. 14. if it presses into Love as into the 2nd Principle: then it becomes God’s child: 15. outside of this, its fire-life is painful. 16. Herein we find the terrible fall of our soul. 17. But Christ has taken it back into himself, 18. and has reborn us again in him; 19. only, that the soul, in a newly created will, should enter with earnestness into the life of Christ, where it is received by God’s children in the 2nd Principle, 20. and lives in the life of God in a gentle delight. 21. For it is a fire in eternal nature, and cannot catch God’s light in its own essences. 22. The Author has this knowledge from God, 23. and sees by the light of the 2nd Principle, 24. which ground is not easily learned without the New Birth <note>original: "Wiedergeburt"</note>. 25. The ignition of the fire stands in the origin in two forms. 26. The will of the eternal Father is attractive, stands in the darkness, and eternally draws itself; 27. 28. because it wants to be free, but cannot: so it conceives within itself another will. 29. Because the darkness then longs for the light: nature originates from this. 30. The 2 forms, harsh and bitter, are attractive, 31. by which the strong stirring and feeling is understood; 32. 33. which the eternal will must suffer; but it conceives another will within itself. 34. These 2 forms are the eternal band, and there must be a counter-will. 35. 36. The angelic world <note>original: "englische Welt," referring to the world of angels, not the English nation</note> is in this place in another quality; 37. but the Word creates the eternal will. 38. Light and darkness come from God’s Word, 39. 40. which is in all things; has the center of birth in itself, 41. and stands in its Maker, who is God himself. 42. This center is the eternal will, 43. which goes forth in the love of God; 44. 45. which the preachers, not recognizing, run in the kingdom of the devil, 46. and are therefore exhorted. 47. Yes, only in the Center of Divine Love is the knowledge of God unlocked by the Holy Spirit, who [proceeds] from the humble...

Therefore, God is not to be sought above the stars, 50. for He is present everywhere; 51. while the Kingdom of Wrath reigns in the center of darkness, 52. and the Word, as the eternal Will, causes Nature: 53. but in the first Will, the Principle of Light is unlocked; 54. and this Word or Will has created everything out of the Father’s essences. <note>ibid. refers to the same source previously cited.</note>

<note>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'S' featuring floral ornaments and vine-work.</note>

SO if we reflect upon the beginning of our life, and wish to hold that against the eternal life which we have in the promise; then we cannot say or find that we are at home in this outward life, for we see the beginning and end of the outward life, as well as the entire fragility and final decay of our bodies: furthermore, we see and know of no return into this life, nor do we have any promise of such from the highest and eternal Good.

2. Since there is now a life in us which is eternal and unbreakable, with which we strive toward the highest Good; and also a life of this world, which is finite and fragile; and also a life in which the <term>Source-Quality</term> <note>Original: "Quall." A central term in Böhme's thought, referring to the inner tension, labor, or "quality" that produces life and sensation, often associated with a "tormenting" or "boiling" energy.</note> and cause of life stands, in which lies the highest danger of eternal perdition, sorrow, and misery; it is therefore necessary for us to reflect on the beginning of life, from whence all this originates and (thus) manifests itself.

3. And if we then reflect on what life is, we find that it is a burning fire that consumes; and when it no longer has anything to consume, it goes out, as can be seen in all fires. For life has its consumption from the body, and the body from food: for if the body no longer has food, the fire of life consumes it, so that it withers and spoils, just as a meadow-flower falls over if it has no water.

4. But if there is yet another life in man that is eternal and unbreakable, namely the <term>Soul</term> <note>Original: "Seele." Here described as a spiritual fire that requires its own specific nourishment to persist.</note>, which is also a fire and must have nourishment just as much as the elemental (mortal) life; then we must reflect on its quality and food, what it may be that gives it food forever, so that it does not go out in eternity.

5. And then thirdly, we find in our soul-life that there is yet a greater hunger within it for another higher and better life, namely for the highest Good,

# III. Concerning the Threefold Life Chapter 1.

Good, which is called the Divine Life, so that the soul does not allow itself to be satisfied with its own food; but rather desires with great longing and yearning the highest and best Good, not merely as a delight, but in its hunger as a sustenance.

6. Thus, we possess in great will and true knowledge the fact that every life desires its mother, from whom that life is born, as its food; just as wood is the mother of fire, which the fire desires, and if it is separated from its mother, it is extinguished: so the earth is the mother of all trees and plants, and they desire her; and water, along with the other elements, is the mother of the earth, otherwise the earth would stand in death, and neither metal nor trees, nor any herb or grass, would grow within or out of it.

7. We see primarily that the elemental life exists in a state of boiling <note>original: "Sude" - referring to a bubbling or fermenting heat</note>, that it is a seething; and if it no longer seethes, it is extinguished: likewise, we know that the stars ignite the elements; and the stars are the fire of the elements, and the sun ignites the stars, so that there is a springing up and seething within one another; but the elemental life is finite and fragile, and the life of the soul is eternal.

8. Since it is then eternal, it must also be from the Eternal, just as the dear Moses quite rightly writes of it: **God** breathed the living breath into man, and so man became a living soul. Genesis 2:7.

9. However, we cannot say that, because man exists in a threefold life, each life is separate, with a distinct form; rather, we find that they are within one another, and yet each life has its effect in its own dominion <note>original: "Regiment" - referring to a sphere of influence or governance</note>, as if in its mother. For just as **God** the Father is everything; (for everything bears witness of Him, and He is present in all places, and is the fullness of all things, and yet the thing does not comprehend Him, nor is the thing **God**, neither of His Spirit, nor of the true Divine Essence; so that one can say of no comprehensible thing: "that is **God**," or "here is **God** more than in other places"; and yet He is truly present, He holds the thing, and the thing does not hold Him; He comprehends the thing,

10. So also is the soul of man breathed in by God: it dwells in the body and is surrounded by the astral and elemental spirit, not merely as a garment covers the body; rather, it is <term>infected<note>original: "inficiret." Used here to mean permeated or influenced, often in a negative or corrupting sense.</note></term> with the astral and elemental spirit, just as the <term>pestilence<note>original: "Pestilenz." Referring to the plague or a contagious disease.</note></term> or another sickness infects the elemental spirit so that it poisons its body, falls down and dies; then the astral torment also breaks away from the soul and consumes itself: because the elemental mother <insert>the physical source of life</insert> breaks apart, the astral spirit no longer has any nourishment; it therefore consumes itself, but the soul remains raw <note>meaning pure or in its original state</note>, because it lives on a different nourishment.

11. Therefore understand us in this way: although the soul is thus captured by the astral and elemental spirit, so that the same torment dwells in the soul; yet the soul has another nourishment and lives in another <term>Principle</term>, and is also of another essence: for its <term>essences<note>original: "Essentien." The fundamental spiritual qualities or "being-ness" of the soul.</note></term> are not from the stars, but have their beginning and bodily union from the eternal bond, from the eternal nature, which is God the Father's before the light of His love; wherein He enters into Himself, and makes for Himself the second <term>Principle</term> in His love, out of which He ever brings forth His eternal Word and Heart from eternity to eternity, where then the holy name of God ever manifests itself, and retains its Divine nature, as one spirit in the other Principle within itself, and dwells in nothing but merely in itself.

12. For although the bond of eternal nature is in Him, yet the Divine Spirit is not subject to the bond: for the Spirit ignites the bond of nature, so that with the power of light in love it becomes illuminated and welling up in the life of the Word of the Heart of God, so that it may be a holy delight and paradise of the Spirit, which is called God.

13. So also is the soul of man from the bond of the eternal manifestation, standing therein eternally, and desires in itself to press into the other <term>Principle</term> toward God, and to satisfy itself on God's power.

14. Because it [the soul] however with its whole being, with its

Thus the Divine life and light come into the soul, and it is **God’s** child: for it stands in its own quality <note>original: "Qual"; Boehme uses this term to mean both a "source-quality" and a state of tension or "anguish" that drives life</note> and life just as **God** the Father Himself stands in the quality of the eternal nature.

16. But you must understand, not as if from the eternal nature alone—such as the soul and the angelic spirits—but from His created will, which has a beginning, as from the Outward: therefore all beings of this world are also transitory.

17. And herein we find the terrifyingly great fall of our souls in our first parents, in that the soul entered into the spirit of this world into a foreign lodging: and has forsaken the Divine light, wherein it was an angel and child of **God**. Therefore it must go out again, out of the

18. But because this was not possible for the soul, the life of **God** came to us in the flesh out of love and grace, and took our human soul back into itself, into the Divine life, into the power of the light, so that we all (every one of us) can penetrate through that same life into a new birth in **God**.

19. For just as we all departed from the life of **God** with Adam’s soul, and inherited the false longing from the souls of our parents (all being generated as if from a single fountain); so has the life of **God** reborn us in *Christ* <note>original: "Christo"</note>, so that in the life of *Christ* we can once again enter into the life of **God**.

20. And as it is now that our soul stands in the bond of the eternal original source <note>original: "Urkundes"; Boehme uses this to mean the primordial ground or the "original record" of existence</note>, infected by the spirit of this world and captured by the wrath of the original source in the life of the eternal fire (as in eternal nature); so we must, each for ourselves, penetrate with our souls into the life of *Christ* toward **God**, into the new rebirth, into the life and spirit of *Christ*. Here, no hypocrisy, outward holiness, or one's own works of merit are of any help; for the poor soul cannot be helped in any other way unless it enters into itself—as into a newly created will—with great and constant earnestness into the life of *Christ*. There, it will be received with great honor by **God** and His children in the second Principle <note>original: "Principio"; the realm of Divine Light and Love</note>, and it will be given the noble, precious treasure: the light of eternal life. This light illuminates the torment and the soul's fire in the first Principle <note>the realm of nature and fire</note>, where the soul essentially stands for eternity with its own essences <note>original: "Essentien"; the fundamental "substances" or "workings" of the soul</note>, and it turns anguish into love; turning the rising and burning (which is the fire’s own right) into a humble, lovely laughter in gentle delight.

21. And thus the soul exists in a state of delight in the Divine life, which I might compare to a lit candle, where the tallow of the candle burns and gives off a joyful shine; in that shine there is no torment, but rather a bright delight, even though the burning glow remains. Yet, you must understand it as if no pain were felt in the glow, but rather that the glow is merely the cause of the light’s appearance; just as one can have no fire without the

# III. Of the Threefold Life Chapter 1

...compare with the Divine; for the Divine nature, from which the Divine life-fire burns, is imbued <note>original: "inficiret"; from the Latin *inficere*, meaning to stain or dye. Here it means the nature is saturated with God's essence.</note> with the love of **God**, so that the light of **God** makes another Principle <term>Principle: Boehme uses this term to describe different planes of reality—the dark fire-world, the light love-world, and the physical world.</term> within itself, in which no nature is felt, for it is the end of nature.

22. Therefore the soul cannot grasp or master the light of **God** in its own essences <term>Essences: the fundamental spiritual "substances" or powers that make up the soul's being.</term>, for it is a fire in the eternal nature, and does not reach the end of nature: for it remains in nature as a created creature out of the eternal nature; and although there is no graspability there, it is instead a spirit in a sevenfold form: and yet in the original source <note>original: "Urkund"; Boehme's term for the primordial ground or the "original record" of existence.</note> not seven but only four are recognized, which hold the eternal bond, and are the torment in the anguish, in which the eternal stands, and from which all the other forms are born, in which **God** and the kingdom of heaven stand; and in the four forms [lie] the anguish and the woe: if they stand bare and alone, then we understand therein the hellish fire and the eternal wrath of **God**.

23. And though we do not know the original source <note>original: "Urkund"</note> of the Divine being (for it has none), yet we know the eternal birth, which never had any beginning. Since it then had no beginning, it is still today as it has ever been from eternity; therefore we may well lay hold of that which we see today and recognize in the light of **God**: and for this reason, no one should regard us as ignorant, because **God** grants us to recognize His own being, which we cannot and should not deny, on pain of losing the Divine light and our eternal salvation; since it is also not possible for any human to take it, unless it be given to him out of **God's** grace in His love. And when it is given to him, the soul stands in the knowledge of the wonders of **God**; it does not speak of distant or foreign things, but of those things in which it stands, and of itself; for it becomes seeing in **God's** light, so that it can know itself.

24. ### III. Of the Threefold Life, Chapter 2.

Since we have shown you such a foundation, we will further show you the ground of the **Birth-giver** <note>original: "Gebärerin." This refers to the generative power of nature or the "genitrix" that continually produces life and form.</note>:
For we see this clearly in this world in the governance of the elements, and much more in ourselves, in our mind—from which the senses arise, through which man’s course, conduct, and all his deeds are performed—that there is a **Birth-giver** who provides this. Now, if there is to be a **Birth-giver**, there must be a **Center** or **Life-Circle** <note>original: "Centrum oder Lebens-Circkel." In Böhme’s cosmology, the "Center" is the point of origin where the divine or natural forces first begin to stir into motion.</note> wherein the Birth-giver takes up her governance: For "Nothing" does not move itself; but where there is a motion that moves all life, it must not be something foreign, since it is the spirit and life in all things, in the growing and the mute as well as in the living.

2. Do not let yourself be deceived by the **hypocrites** <note>original: "Gleißner." Often used by Böhme to describe religious or academic pretenders who possess outward show but no inner truth.</note> who are merely **scholars of history** <note>original: "Historien-Gelehrte." Böhme uses this to describe those who learn about God and nature only through books and rote memorization of the past, rather than through direct spiritual experience.</note> and parade about with foreign languages, wishing to be honored for them, though they do not understand them in the least. They do not even understand their **mother-tongue**; if they understood it rightly, and the spirits of the letters, they would recognize nature therein.

3. It is **Pride** <note>original: "Hoffart." One of Böhme's primary "sins" of the intellect.</note> that forbids you from searching, so that you might not find, and so that she (Pride), in her **crowned little hat** <note>original: "gecröneten Hütlein." Likely a mocking reference to academic or clerical caps (the doctor’s beret or a mitre).</note>, may hover like a proud woman over the wonders of GOD: for the Devil wants it so, that he might not be recognized; they are blinder than the simple layman.

4. If you wish to search, then knock, so that the right door may be opened to you; and search in the fear and love of GOD, and you shall indeed find. Do not let the blasphemy of the proud lead you astray: For when the right door is opened to you, you will see how they are so blind; their pride has blinded the world, so that everyone looks only upon the art of **eloquence** in foreign languages and thinks they understand it. Thus they rule over the souls of men, even though their knowledge stands in vain doubt, as can be seen in their quarreling.

5. So I say again, one should not entrust his soul to men of hypocrisy: for the soul does not stand in this world, but in the **original source of the essence of all essences** <note>original: "Urkunde des Wesens aller Wesen." This phrase suggests the primal record or foundational reality from which all existence springs.</note>, and is in the **Center** of the eternal bond, wherein God, the Kingdom of Heaven, and the Kingdom of Hell stand; and if it reaches God’s love in the light (which dwells in its Center), it may well [reach] the

30. For every anguish has a will to escape the torment. And that is the natural right of anguish: to drive itself out, and yet it cannot; rather, the torment only becomes more expansive and greater through this, just as one understands in a raging, anxious wound, where the limb works within its **essences** <note>original: "Essentien" — Böhme uses this term to describe the active, driving spiritual powers or qualities within a being.</note> to cast the torment away, and in that very work of the essences, it only grows larger, and the torment merely swells up in the **Sulfur-Spirit**; the more the essences resist, the larger the **wheel of anguish** <note>original: "Rad der Angst" — a central Böhmean concept describing the restless, circular motion of the lower qualities of nature before they are transformed by light.</note> becomes; I leave this for the senses to contemplate.

31. Thus I give you nature to contemplate, which, if you reflect upon it, you cannot contradict: for this is in all things and has its birthright thus; and nature stands thus in the **Center** <note>original: "Centro"</note> in four forms.

32. First, in the harsh, strict attraction, which is called **Harshness**, and creates within itself a strict coldness.

33. And then second, the pulling is its **sting** <note>original: "Stachel" — the second property of nature, representing motion, agitation, and conflict.</note>, which rages in the harshness and breaks the hardness, and creates the wheel of innumerable essences, within which the wonders are born.

34. But the **flash** <note>original: "Blitz"</note> of the freedom of the eternal will, which sharpens itself in the harshness and becomes a consuming fire, breaks its wheel, as it penetrates instantly like a flash and terrifies its mother, the harshness; she then loses her hard right and is natured into a **sharpness** <note>original: "Schärfe"</note> similar to salt. In this sharpness, the sting also loses its own right and becomes bitter, for it has two forms within itself: raging, and also the fire-flash. These resemble **sulfur**, and it is the power of the fire's ignition, for the torment of the fire stands within it.

Sharpness makes the third **property** <note>original: "Gestalt" — Böhme's term for the active qualities or "forms" of nature.</note> in nature; for in the harshness and out of the raging, it creates the bitter sting; in the harsh anguish, it creates a **Sulfur-Spirit**, in which the flash stands; and it is the soul or the eternal life of the four properties. For the anguish again creates within itself a desire to flee from the anguish, and yet there is nothing there that might flee; rather, this is how it is in the **center** <note>original: "Centro"</note>, and here it is no longer called the **center**.

36. The fourth property is the transformation of the hard harshness, when the terror of the flash frightens the dark harshness (or: hardness), so that it is overcome, becoming soft and as if dead, where it becomes **Salt** <note>original: "Sal"</note>, and yet retains the law of harsh attraction.

37. Thus the four properties of nature are now no longer called the **center**, although they still have the **center** within them at their origin; rather they are called **Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt** <note>original: "Sulphur, Mercurius und Sal" — Böhme adopts these three alchemical terms to describe the fundamental energies of all matter: Sulfur (the fire/soul), Mercury (the movement/spirit), and Salt (the physical substance/body).</note>: For the Sulfur-Spirit is the soul of the four properties, because it has the fire within it, and the anguish creates another will within itself, so that the four properties have an eternal will within themselves that is their own. For that same will is to flee out from the four properties, beyond nature, and to ignite nature in the fire, and thus to exist in terrible power, as can be perceived in the devils who live in this will, as we shall set forth hereafter.

38. Thus understand us rightly, what the ancient wise men understood by these three words, **Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt**: although they were not able to grasp the high light in its fullness, they nevertheless had enough of it in their understanding within the light of this world—that is, in the third **principle** <note>original: "Principio" — Böhme’s term for the three distinct realms of reality: the dark world, the light world, and the physical world.</note>, which has the same meaning and concept; only they did not understand the **principles** <note>original: "Principia"</note>, otherwise they would have known God. But thus they remained as pagans with their understanding in the light of this world; for they discovered the soul of the four properties in the light of the sun-force, and the other **principle** was not revealed to them any further.

However, in this world—which is the <term>third Principle</term> <note>Böhme's term for the material, visible world, which sits between the worlds of light (heaven) and darkness (the abyss).</note>—they are not understood in their very earnest essences. This is because the power of the sun within the elements tempers everything, so that the essences do not exist in fierce torment <note>original: "Qual" — a word Böhme uses to imply both agony and the "welling up" of a fountain.</note>, but rather in the delight of a friendly life. This is just as the light from the <term>second Principle</term> <note>The divine world of light and the heart of God.</note>—which is the light from the Word and Heart of **God** the Father—illuminates the four forms in the center of the angelic spirits, so that they are friendly, lovely, and quite blissful within their own center.

48. And you may well consider the fall of the devils, who lost the light of the heart of **God** and who must now exist within the four forms of the original source in such anxious torment, as was mentioned above.

49. Likewise, the soul of man was breathed into man from this eternal bond and illuminated by the light of **God**. However, in the fall of Adam, it departed from the eternal light of the heart of **God** and entered into the light of this world. It now has this to expect: that if it does not enter back into the light of **God**, and the light of this world then breaks away from it <note>Meaning at the moment of physical death.</note>, it must remain simply within the four forms, outside the light of **God**, in the earnest "birth-of-life" alongside the devils.

50. For the four forms without the eternal light are the abyss, the wrath of **God**, and hell. The terrifying flash of fire in the "wheel of breaking" <note>A metaphor for the churning, restless activity of nature before it finds the peace of divine light.</note> during the rising of <term>Mercury</term> within the sulfur-spirit is their light—a light which they must awaken within themselves. Otherwise, their spirit stands in eternal darkness and is a living form of the abyss, a regime of earnest torment which rises up in the fire-flash above **God** and the kingdom of heaven, yet never reaches it, nor sees it, nor feels it. For it is a <term>Principle</term> that neither this world nor the angelic world can grasp, and yet it is not separated by distance or place.

Latin for "Let it be done," referring to the creative command in Genesis.</note>, all things are grasped, and the Spirit of the Word forms them in the <term>Center</term> <note>original: "Centro."</note> of that same essence, in which the Father moves and speaks through the Word, so that it is and remains in being. For what is formed out of the Eternal, that is spirit and is eternal, such as the angels and the souls of humanity.

65. If we then seem silent and unintelligible to you in this description—since the concept does not lie in the spirit of this world—we want to show you the other three heavenly forms, how they are born, in which primarily God, the kingdom of heaven, paradise, and the angelic world are understood, so that the reader might be brought to understanding.

66. It is not to be understood that the Godhead takes on a beginning and change in this way; no. Rather, I write in a manner so that one may learn to understand the Divine Being, for we cannot use angelic words. And even if we did use them, everything in this world appears as a creature, and moreover, to the earthly mind, it appears earthly. For we are also no more than a particular [part] of the whole and cannot speak completely, but only in <term>piecemeal</term> <note>original: "Stückwerck." This is a scriptural reference to 1 Corinthians 13:9, "we know in part." Böhme reminds the reader that human language is too limited to describe the infinite God all at once.</note>; the reader should consider this.

67. For the Divine Mind in the heart of God is alone a whole, and nothing else; for everything else stands in the essences, and God alone is free, and nothing else. Therefore, we speak in pieces and grasp the whole within the mind; for we have no tongue to express it, so we lead the reader as if on a ladder.

68. If we then want to write or speak rightly of God, we must speak of the light and the flame of love, for therein is God understood.

69. We cannot say that the source of the fire is the light; rather, we see that it shines out of the fire. Now we have told you of the fire’s <term>original source</term> <note>original: "Urstande." The primal foundation or origin.</note>, how it is born in the wheel of essences in the hard, anxious sharpness, and takes its glimpse from eternal freedom, where freedom is driven into nature, so that out of freedom comes a <term>torment</term> <note>original: "Qual." Böhme often plays on the word "Qual" (torment/pain) and its relation to "Quelle" (source/spring) and "Qualität" (quality), suggesting that the "tension" of existence is what produces life.</note>, which is fire.

70. So we have also reported to you how the lightning-flash penetrates straight through the wheel of the essences and makes a ♰ <note>The cross symbol represents the intersection of the eternal world and the natural world, or the turning point where the dark "fire" of nature is transformed into the "light" of the spirit.</note>,

84. Thus the other Word or growth of Love dwells in the first will, and is its true fulfillment, which it desires: for it is gentle, lovely, and friendly, and is the power and **Heart** of the first will, from which the eternal desire always stands in essence and will.

If we now wish to explore the lovely birth of Love—how it expresses itself and what its origin is—we must fathom the Center <term>Centrum: the inner core or point of origin from which all spiritual and natural life emerges</term> most inwardly. We must take up the sixth form of nature <term>Gestalt der Natur: one of the seven qualities Böhme describes as the building blocks of existence</term>, which is Mercury <note>original: "Mercurium," referring here to the spiritual principle of motion, vibration, and sound</note>, in which sound is born; thus, in the birth of Love, we shall find tone, resonance, and song. Furthermore, the five senses—seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and feeling—are found there, through which life is then understood, as well as pain and torment, just as much as joy and love, the desire for good, and also the desire for evil. Although in itself nothing in nature is rejectable; both must exist, otherwise God would not be manifest, and everything would be a still Nothing. The entire essence exists together in the one God: no one has made or birthed anything for Him; He alone, in His eternal will, which He Himself is, creates the birthing mother <note>original: "Gebärerin," the feminine principle of nature that brings forth form</note>.

40. 41. For this time is like a field, which is the seventh seal of eternal nature, within which the six seals open themselves with their powers and wonders and pour out their wrath. Thus, one seal after another has opened itself, but the wonders within the powers of the seals have remained misunderstood by human reason.

For we are the image of the Godhead, in which the Spirit of **God** reveals His wonders. And let yourself be rightly instructed: **God** the Father has reborn us in Christ, so that we should enter again with our imagination into the Word, as into the center of His light-flaming Heart, so that the Holy Spirit might again go out from us with powers, wonders, and deeds, as was seen with Christ’s Apostles.

### Chapter 3. Of Man.

82. Therefore, take note, you who sleep, and wake up; the day is breaking, it is high time, so that the Wrath in **Babel** <note>In Böhme’s writing, "Babel" represents the confused and corrupt institutional church, characterized by division and spiritual pride.</note> does not seize you. Great seriousness is at hand; cease your quarreling over the **Chalice of Christ** <note>A reference to the intense theological disputes over the nature of the Eucharist or Lord's Supper.</note>; you shall be found as fools before **GOD**. It does not depend on your resolutions, that you band together and decide: "Thus we want to believe, thus we want to have it, so that the **Church of GOD** may be preserved"; while the other party speaks against it and calls each other **Heretics**. Thus, in your pride, you lead the blind **Laity** captive in your **strife of doubt (devilish strife)** <note>original: "Zweifels- (Teufels-) Zancke." Böhme puns on the similarity between "Zweifel" (doubt) and "Teufel" (devil), suggesting that theological dispute is diabolical in nature.</note>. 83. Oh, you proud, blind people, how you allow yourselves to be seduced by conceit without **God's Spirit**! You have filled them with blasphemy, and they have ridden upon the **Dragon** in pure **hypocrisy** <note>original: "Gleißnerey." An older term for outward religious show or Pharisaism that lacks inner faith.</note>, in greed, pride, and false teaching; you have glittered on the outside, but inside you have been full of the **Devil**.

For the layman does not know what he does; he merely plays the fiddle you provide <note>original: "er fiedelt auf eurer Geigen." A metaphor meaning the common people simply follow the tune or agenda set by the clergy.</note>, and would rather lose his life than turn from **Error** into the **Life of Christ**.

85. Oh, you simple **Holiness**, why do you not accept **Christ**, your faithful Shepherd, as your shepherd, and let the wolves go? You need not quarrel at all over **Christ’s Kingdom**; the wolves have no power to take it from you or to give it to you. Nor do you need to ask, "Where is **Christ**? Is He in the **Supper** and in **Baptism**, is He in the hearing of the **Preaching Office**?"—as people today so strictly insist.

86. Just look within, and incline your heart, senses, and mind toward **Christ**, so that **Christ** is born in you. Then you have **Christ**, **Baptism**, the **Sacrament**, and the **Holy Spirit** in all places; you have Him in the hearing of the **Divine Word**.

87. The **Covenants** and **Testaments of Christ**, which are used for a long time without **Faith**, are only hidden **Seals**. But if you are born in **Christ**, then they are **Seals** opened to you in your **Heart** and in your **Soul**; it is all—

### III. Of the Threefold Life, Chapter 4

7. Now the <term>essences<note>original: "Essentien." In Böhme's system, these are the active, living powers or spiritual energies that constitute all matter and spirit.</note></term> desire nothing but the preservation and building of the body: for the body is their food, and is the entire being of all beings, a constant hunger and fulfillment, and then from that which is filled, a rebirthing, as one may observe.

8. Every form of the spirit hungers for the others: and as it obtains the other, another form arises from it, yet the first does not pass away; rather, the second forms itself within the first into another <term>quality<note>original: "Qual." Böhme uses this term to denote a "source-spring" or a "working property." It is a pun on the German words "Quelle" (source) and "Qual" (torment or tension), implying that every quality arises from an inner struggle or movement.</note></term>, and yet both remain within one another, each keeping its own property. We have written of nature in this way as consisting of six forms, how one proceeds from the other, and how each is the cause of the other being born, and yet each retains its property in the other. And even though they now stand within one another in six forms, there is still no place of rest, but rather a constant desiring of all six forms, like a great hunger. From this, the "will" is always born. But since there is nothing where rest might be, except for the still eternity—and such a thing cannot be grasped or found within the wheel of the fiery essences—hungry nature seeks within its mother, namely in the desire of <term>astringency<note>original: "Herbigkeit." This refers to the first property of nature: the harsh, contracting, and "harsh" force that pulls inward to create substance.</note></term>. And this astringency catches the desire of the essences and holds it. Thus, all the essences of hunger stand held within the harsh mother, for she is their only rest, which she fills again (continually) with that which is in her, namely with herself.

9. Within this lies the dominion of a spirit: For nature does not stand alone in seven forms, but from every desire a "will" can be born again, within which the essences stand again, but changeable according to the desire of that same will. In this stands omnipotence and the wonders, of which no number can be found, as you may see in the creation of the world.

10. But when the eternal being desires a certain goal or measure—against which or beyond which it desires nothing higher, different, or further—then it has birthed for itself the **Heart**, which is the end of nature, and the **Heart** is the fulfillment of the Eternal.

11. Now, however, the Heart of nature is also not graspable, and nature nevertheless remains within itself in darkness, and the Heart within itself in the light, and neither would be manifest:

12. Now we see in the angelic world, as well as in this world, that the seventh form of nature is a substantial form, from which the embodiment came to be through the <term>Word Fiat<note>original Latin: "Verbum Fiat." This refers to the creative "Let there be" of God in Genesis, which Böhme views as a spiritual "attraction" or "compaction" of will into matter.</note></term>; and we establish that this also exists in two forms: one in the darkness and the other in the light. 13. As noted previously, this is Böhme’s pun on "Quelle" (source) and "Qual" (torment/tension), signifying the dynamic struggle within nature.</note></term>, and causes a quality of anguish, longing, and desire to be within it. For the darkness itself has no desire; rather, desire is born within it, and the darkness causes the desire to arise—namely, a desire to be free from the darkness.

14. Thus, the desire labors so greatly for <term>freedom<note>original: "Freyheit." In Böhme's philosophy, "Freedom" often refers to the "Unground" or the divine realm of absolute stillness and liberty that exists before and beyond the friction of nature.</note></term>, until the anguish in the piercing desire perceives freedom within itself—and yet it is not freedom; and even if it were, it still stands within the harshness of the anguish and is called Fire. At this point, the desire can go no higher, but must suffocate within itself and sink down into the source-quality. And the sharpness of the <term>fire-flash<note>original: "Feuer-Blitz." This is the moment of ignition or enlightenment where the dark desire breaks through into light, or where the soul is "struck" by divine realization.</note></term> in the sharp freedom retains its right as a still quality that stands in the sharpness of freedom. And this sinking of the anguish is to be compared to a death, out of which the fire-life is born. This same death provides the weight; for compared to the fire of freedom, it is like a drowning within itself. In its sinking, the anguish becomes <term>material<note>original: "materialisch." This describes the process of spiritual forces condensing into substance or "matter."</note></term>, so that in this death, one perceives the entire form of the quality tangibly—or perceptibly, I might say. And this perceptibility is the <term>corporeality<note>original: "Leiblichkeit." The physical or bodily manifestation of spiritual principles.</note></term> of the darkness, and the fire of freedom in the fierce flash is its spirit and life. Hereby it is suggested to you that you look into yourselves, and see that the fire creates the feeling within the harshness of the dead corporeality; for without fire, no body has any feeling, as you can see in the earth and stones.

15. Now it is further shown to you that the body or the substance is not such a death that is worth nothing, or merely a useless thing: for the sinking (suffocation) drives its torment downward and provides weight, and the fire [drives] upward and provides spirit, life, and mobility.

16. Now, in the middle between these is the <term>Center<note>original Latin: "Centrum." Böhme uses this to describe the focal point of spiritual birth where opposing forces meet.</note></term> of the desiring anguish; this is a cause of the upper part, namely the fire, and also of the lower part, namely the substance. Since the <term>Center</term> cannot go upward nor downward, and yet is driving with desire, it drives crosswise, and the entire form stands like a tree in growth. For it appears in the Center as a ✠ <note>The cross symbol represents the four directions of expansion—up, down, and crosswise—that Böhme sees as the fundamental geometry of creation.</note> out of which the <term>Essences<note>original Latin: "Essentien." These are the active, driving qualities or "seeds" of a thing's nature.</note></term> of desire break out, just like a tree or growth, as I might interpret it; and yet it is not a growing, but rather an out-driving from itself, like a pricking in the dead substance.

17. And we give you here earnestly to understand that the torment in the <term>Center</term> (out of which the fire goes upward into the substance, and death sinks downward, and the <term>Essences</term> [go] crosswise) gives birth to another will: to set both death and also the fire in its sharpness, along with the <term>Essences</term> of the will, into freedom. And that same will attains freedom in the fire and causes the fire to shine brightly and creates a delight.

18. And this other conceived will is called <term>Tincture<note>original Latin: "Tinctur." In alchemy and Böhme's theology, the Tincture is a transformative, spiritual power that brings light, color, and vitality to raw, dark matter.</note></term>, for it is a luster in the darkness and has the power of life, and it turns green through the death of the substance and stills the anguish. It has, however, no <term>Essences</term> within itself, but it is the ornament and power of the <term>Essences</term>; it is the delight of life. It cannot retreat from the anxious sharpness, and yet the sharpness does not hold it either; for it is free, and a flower of life. It is not gentle or sweet, but it resembles a burning sulfur <note>original: "Schwefel." Böhme often associates sulfur with the "sulfurous" or fiery, expansive quality of the soul's energy.</note> where the fire receives a luster, which otherwise in the <term>Center</term> in the anguish is black and dark.

20. Behold the <term>Center<note>original Latin: "Centrum." Böhme uses this term to describe the focal point where spiritual and material forces meet to create life.</note></term> of the Earth, which **God** created through the Word, right out of the Center of the deep eternity, out of the darkness, out of the Center of the desiring will—not from some specific location, but out of the vastness and the depth. Wherever the Word gave itself into the <term>Ethers<note>original Latin/Greek: "Æthern." These are the subtle, celestial regions or spiritual atmospheres above the physical world.</note></term>, there the Center was in all places, and is still so, and remains so in eternity: for it has been so from eternity. This is the beginning: that the Word conceived a will in the darkness, to reveal the darkness with all its forms of the wonders of **God** the Father in His nature, which He brings forth in His eternal will within the desire.

21. And we show you this: Look at the earth, stones, and metals; they are all together as if they were dead and have weight; moreover, they are in the darkness, and yet they have their light within them, namely the noble <term>Tincture<note>original Latin: "Tinctur." In Böhme’s alchemy, this is the hidden spiritual essence or "blood" of nature that gives matter its color, life, and medicinal power.</note></term>, which is their light and life, in which the ore-stones grow—those in which the <term>Tincture</term> is powerful.

22. So you see also how the <term>Sulfur-fire<note>original German: "Schwefel-Feuer." This refers to the active, burning principle of nature that drives transformation.</note></term> is the conqueror of nature, in which the <term>Tincture</term> arises; and thus, through the death of nature, it flourishes in stones and metals, and brings forth the essence of luster and brilliance within nature, as can be seen in gold and silver, as well as in all gleaming metals. Therein we also perceive at the same time the poisonous anxiety of the darkness, and also the harsh death of the darkness in the stern <term>Matter<note>original Latin: "Materia."</note></term> of the mixture, as those who work with such things understand.

23. We also see how the <term>Tincture</term> can bring the lowest thing in death to its highest adornment, such as a lowly metal into gold, and all this because of the great power of eternity. For the strict power of fire pleased him more than the gentleness in the still bliss: therefore he was also thrust back into the dark **Matrix**, into the anxious **mind**, into the sinking of death.

The creative, maternal force of nature that produces all forms of existence.</note></term> to be considered; there one finds all the forms that can be fathomed in the whole of nature.

Latin for "The Word of the Lord."</note></term>, as if to the heart of God; thus the spirit is conceived and born in God's love.

### III. Of the Threefold Life Ch. 4.

...Life of Man is written, it will be very useful to him; only then will he rightly come into this understanding, so that he may then esteem it as a great treasure <note>original: "Kleinod." Literally a jewel or precious gem; a term Böhme uses for spiritual pearls of wisdom.</note>.

60. For the <term>Mind<note>original: "Gemüthe." In Böhme’s writing, this refers to the seat of the soul’s desires and the origin of the will, more expansive than the modern "intellect."</note></term> does not cease to search until it reaches the innermost ground, which is indicated here. But if it does not reach the ground, it sinks into the abyss <note>original: "Grund." Böhme uses "Grund" (ground) and "Ungrund" (abyss/foundationless) to describe the depths of God.</note> and cannot grasp it; then doubt, unbelief, and contempt enter the Mind. We wish to warn the reader of this: do not trifle with this high mystery, otherwise the Spirit of God will be blasphemed.

61. And it happens to the Mind as it did to Lucifer: when he saw the greatest mysteries of the Godhead standing in such <term>humility<note>original: "Demuth." For Böhme, humility is the essential nature of the "Light" world, whereas pride characterizes the "Fire" world.</note></term>, he took offense and entered into the harsh power of fire. He wanted to rule over God through his own wit; God was to be subject to him. He wanted to be the master of the forms in nature, and therefore he became a devil.

62. For the Kingdom of Heaven, with the angelic world and the power of God’s heart, stands in gentleness and humility.

63. For the Light stands in gentleness: and although it manifests itself out of the <term>Center<note>original: "Centro." Böhme often uses the Latin "Centrum" to describe the core of a spiritual principle.</note></term> of fire—which is the <term>severity<note>original: "Schärfe." Literally "sharpness." In Böhme’s alchemy, this represents the bracing, contractive quality of the first principle of fire before it is transformed into light.</note></term> of God—it nevertheless establishes its Center in great gentleness. For the <term>Freedom<note>original: "Freyheit." This refers to the "Ungrund," the divine nothingness or liberty that exists beyond the mechanical workings of Nature.</note></term> outside of Nature is the end of Nature, and in that Freedom dwells the Light, like the radiance of a still delight. And the Word, arising from the powers of Nature, is the fire of the Light, from which the shine goes forth that illuminates the entire depth of the Father. Thus it is one essence within itself, but with three distinctions, where each distinction has a Center and may be called a Person.

64. For the Father generates Nature out of the eternal, still Freedom, which He Himself is. In that stillness He is not yet called "Father," but insofar as He is desiring and conceives a will within Himself to be the Begetter of Nature, He is recognized as a Father, from whom all beings proceed, as from His first will through all subsequent wills.

65. Just as a human Mind is but one will, which is desiring, yet it conceives within itself—out of that one (eternal) will—countless many wills, one proceeding from the other; thus we see and find that the first will...

In Böhme's thought, "Grimm" is not just anger, but the fierce, consuming fire of raw existence and nature's strict laws.</note></term>, and yet they are not separated. 68. The spiritual "atoms" or qualities that form the basis of all reality.</note>, out of the forms of nature—as the Life of nature. And He is called a **Person** because He is a self-subsisting Being that does not belong to the birth of nature, but is nature’s life and understanding. And He is called the **Father’s Heart** because He is the power in the center of nature, and stands in nature like a heart in the body, which gives power and understanding to all the limbs. And He is called **God’s Light** because the light is ignited in Him and takes its origin in Him. And He is called the **Radiance of God** because He creates a shine in the eternal still freedom, which originates from the sharpness of eternal nature, as mentioned before. And He is called the **Father’s Love** because the first will of the Father toward the mother <note>original: "Gebärerin." Literally "the female-birther." ### III. Of the Threefold Life Ch. 4.

...His dear Heart desires; and this is in the Father's will, the most beloved above *Nature*, though it is still His own *Being*. This is called a "Wonder" because He is the Creator of all things, through whom everything is brought forth from the *Center* of the Father's *Essences* into the Light and into *Being*, so that the Father's *Nature* stands in great wonder.

69. This is the distinction: that Father and Son are called two *Persons*, and yet are only one **GOD** in one *Being*. The Father is the begetter of *Nature*, in whom it is born through His will out of desire; but His Heart separates itself from *Nature* and is not gripped by *Nature*. It leads its own separate *Center* as Love, while the Father is Wrath. In the Father’s sharpness is fire, and in the Son’s sharpness is light; yet they are within one another like fire and light.

70. But just as fire wants to be free or else it is smothered—and yet it burns out of the dark, <term>fierce<note>original: "grimmen." Although it burns out of many *Materials*, it still gives off only one *Quality*: heat and light.

71. Understand us in this way regarding the Godhead as well: the Son is in the Father's light *Eternity*, and also in His contained will, within His *Nature*. He is only one *Quality* that burns in love and light, and is the Father's radiance and glory. He cannot be separated from the Father or be at odds with Him, for there is only one Will in Him, which is called the Desire of Mercy, and it ignites everything that attaches itself to Him.

72. And the *Holy Spirit* is the third *Person*, whom I previously called the <term>Mercurial Spirit<note>In the alchemical language Böhme often uses, Mercury represents the principle of movement, vibration, and communication. It is the "voice" or "action" of the spirit.</note></term> within the Divine *Nature* because of its properties. You see that every will is still within itself, and every light is also still; but the sound makes the will manifest. The sound then stands before the will and creates another *Center*. For the sound is captured and carried forth, but the will is not. You see this in a word: how it is captured and carried forth, having been born out of the sound.

73. Thus you also know how the sound takes its origin in the heart and goes out from the *Essences* of the will, and is captured in the mouth, and yet expresses itself from the heart—

Man is pulled by two; 30. and without rebirth no one can behold God. 31. The hypocritical art of logic is of no use here, but is only an error.

Chapter 5. Of Man.

# The Second Gate into the Holy Ternary, to be Highly Contemplated.
<note>original: "Ternarium Sanctum." This term refers to the divine, heavenly environment or the "body" of the Trinity, which Böhme describes as the spiritual "ground" of all existence.</note>

1. I know well, you **sophist** <note>Böhme uses this term to describe academic theologians or scholars who rely on worldly logic and intellectual pride rather than direct spiritual revelation.</note>, that you will accuse me of pride for this—that I, being one of the lowly and small in this world, should climb so high into the depths. But it is said to you that you look upon the wisdom of this world; I, however, pay no heed to it, for it gives me no joy. But I rejoice in this: that my soul floats in wonders to **God’s** praise, that I recognize His wondrous work, in which my soul delights as if in its mother. For every spirit speaks only of its mother, of whose food it eats, and in whose **source-quality** <note>original: "Qual." A central concept for Böhme, this word combines the meanings of source, quality, and the labor or "torment" of existence. It refers to the internal energy that makes a thing what it is.</note> it lives.

2. If I now recognize these wonders, should I then be silent? Indeed, I was born for this, as were all creatures: that they should reveal **God’s** wonders. So I labor in what is mine, and another in what is his, and you, proud **sophist**, also in what is yours.

3. We all stand in **God’s** field and grow toward **God’s** wondrous work and glory—the godless as well as the pious—but every plant grows in its own **source-quality**. When the reaper shall mow it down, every one shall come into its own barns, and every **source-quality** shall receive its own. Then the field shall be revealed in its **essences** from which we have grown; for there are two **centers** in eternity, and each shall harvest its own fruit within itself.

It truly signifies the Spirit of **God**, of which **Christ** says that when He comes, He will convict the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment (John 16:8-11).

5. Of sin, because they live in **hypocrisy** <note>original: "Gleißnerey." They do not wish to be born again, but reveal only the wonders in the wrath of vain **hypocrisy**.

52. 54. For everything is contained herein; just like a wrestling match, where one is on top and powerful, and then is overcome, and another of a different essence arises. 56. When I speak of the **Virgin of the Wisdom of God**, I do not mean a thing restricted to one place or with an end, just as I speak of the Trinity; rather, I mean the entire depth of the Godhead without end or number.

57. But every **divine creature**, such as the angels and the souls of men, has the Virgin of God's Wisdom within them like an image in the light of life—understand this to be within the substantiality of the spirit, where the Trinity dwells within itself.

58. For we grasp the Trinity in this image, as in the Virgin of Wisdom for ourselves; understand that outside of our own person we see only the majesty of the Godhead. For the creature does not grasp the Trinity by direct sight, but the spirit of the soul, which stands in the **Divine Center** <term>Centro</term> <note>original: "Centro." The point of origin or the heart of spiritual manifestation.</note>, grasps it, though not perfectly.

59. For a **soul-spirit** is from one form of nature, and yet it can bring forth all forms of nature within itself.

67. Every being has its own form: the reader might understand only one form within these four shapes, so we wish to show him the distinction. The focal point or heart of divine manifestation.</note>, which goes through all forms: It goes through the element, and through the substantiality, and also through heaven, like the growth of a pleasure-garden: That is why Adam was in Paradise while in this world.

Literally "three-number," Böhme's term for the Triune nature of God.</note> of **God**, its light is the glance of the Majesty of the Trinity: it is only a matter of the external; when the four elements break apart in man, the soul is already in Paradise, or in the abyss of the <term>Center</term> <note>original: "Centri." The core point of origin for either the light or dark spiritual realms.</note> in the dark <term>Matrix</term> <note>original: "Matrice." The generative "womb" or source from which all things are born.</note>; all according to that in which the soul has grown during this time on earth.

127. If she has set her <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "Imagination." For Böhme, this is not just "make-believe," but the creative power of the soul's desire to shape its own spiritual reality.</note> in **God**, then she has grown in Paradise, and only the swollen, dark body of this time has hidden her.

# III. Of the Threefold Life Chap. 5. #

128. If, however, it <note>The soul.</note> has grown in fierce wrath, in falsehood, or in the pride of flying out beyond Paradise, then it flies out in pride within the fierce <term>Matrix</term> <note>original: "Matrice." In Böhme’s thought, the "Matrix" is the generative womb or source from which a specific quality of life is born—either the light-world or the dark-world.</note> beyond Paradise and cannot enter into the gentleness: there it remains in Hell with the proud devil.

129. For after this life there is no further rebirth: for the four elements with the external <term>Principle</term> <note>original: "Principio." This refers to the physical world of time and space, governed by the four elements.</note> are gone, wherein the mother <note>The soul’s generative power.</note> stood in her working and creating; she has nothing more to expect after this time, except for when, at the end of this world, this Principle shall go into the <term>Ether</term> <note>original: "Æther." A term for the refined, non-material state that remains after the physical elements are dissolved.</note>. Then the substantiality that has been from eternity will be free again, and she will receive a body again out of her own mother, out of her own <term>torment</term> <note>original: "Qual." Böhme uses this term to describe both "quality/source" and "agony." It refers to the internal tension or "vibration" that constitutes a soul's being.</note>: then all her works will appear before her in her mother.

130. For the <term>Last Day</term> <note>original: "Jüngste Tag." Judgment Day.</note> is nothing other than the awakening of those who have fallen asleep and the breaking of death, which resides in the four elements: for the covering must be removed, and everything that is born of the Eternal must green and live again.

131. But whatever is born of death, such as from the four elements—like the cattle and all life of the four elements—that shall receive a body no more; for its spirit also stood only in the four elements, and it breaks apart along with the four elements, and only the figure of the elemental being remains, as if from the four <term>out-births</term> <note>original: "Ausgeburten." Secondary manifestations of a deeper reality.</note>.

132. But whatever is from the Eternal, from the eternal <term>Life-Center</term> <note>original: "Lebens-Centro."</note>, that is and remains eternal: also all words and works that have been born out of the Eternal remain in the essence of the figure; for they cannot remain eternally in spirit and power, because a word of the spirit has not come from eternity, but originated in the external Principle.

133. Therefore, every spirit will have joy and sorrow in its works and words in eternity, all according to whether it is in a place in a certain <term>torment</term> <note>Again, "Qual" as the internal state of the soul.</note>: for when the spirit reflects upon its torment, why it is in this place, then the quality of its works and words rises up within it, and gives it joy or sorrow, according to the place and the quality it is in, each in its own.

134. But know this, that the <term>reborn in Christ</term> <note>original: "Neugebornen in Christo."</note>

# Chapter 5. Of Mankind. #

134. 137. For his body was from the earth, and created out of the earth, yet he was not "earth"; for he was created out of the earth's <term>Matrix</term> <note>original: "Matrice." 141. For the four elements are all within one another; and their foundation, upon which they stand, is the fire of the fierce wrath of God, in which the devils dwell, as mentioned above.

142. Thus the new Adam, Christ, had to go into the abyss of the four elements, as into the hellish fire of wrath, and pass through the hell of wrath through death, and lead the human soul back into the Paradise of God.

143. And for that reason, the new Adam, Christ, was tempted for forty days in the wilderness, to see if He could withstand in the paradisiacal <term>torment</term> <note>original: "Qual." 144. For He also bore the earthly image at the same time, so the new heavenly [image] had to overcome the earthly one: and the soul had to enter into the new heavenly body again, so that the earthly one merely clung to it.

145. Adam was also created this way in the beginning: he was meant to eat from Paradise; that same <term>torment</term> <note>or "source-quality"</note> was meant to rule over the earthly elements. 149. Depart from the languages in Babel: for in Jerusalem we all speak only one language: Babel burns in the fire, Amen.

### III. Of the Threefold Life, Chapter 6.

4. For just as God from eternity has held the essence <note>original: "Wesen." In Böhme’s vocabulary, this refers to the fundamental substance or "being" of a thing.</note> of this world in His Word, which He has always spoken into Wisdom; so we also have it in our word, and we speak it into the wonders of His Wisdom.

5. For God is Himself the Essence of all essences, and we are as gods in Him, through whom He reveals Himself.

6. You see that a beast can express nothing; it lacks this because it is not from the Eternal, as man is. It bleats and cries out according to the form in the manifestation <note>original: "Ausgeburt," literally an "out-birthing." This refers to the physical expression of spiritual or elemental forces.</note> of the four elements, and has no higher spirit than the elements; although its fleeting senses come from the stars <note>original: "Gestirne." Böhme believed animals were governed by astrological influences rather than possessing an eternal, reasoning soul.</note>, which are nonetheless silent and without a concept of essence.

7. Thus we wish to fundamentally present to you the ground of the heavens, stars, and elements, so that you may see what is heavenly or earthly; what is perishable and mortal, and what is eternal and lasting. This is the end for which we have undertaken to write this book; not for the glory of our own high knowledge—which is in God and is of no use to us in this world—but out of love in Christ. As a servant and minister of Christ, I seek the lost sheep from the house of God’s Israel. For the Lord holds both the willing and the doing in His hands; we are capable of nothing, nor does our earthly reason understand anything. We are surrendered in the Mother’s womb <note>original: "Mutter Schooß." This refers to the Divine Wisdom (Sophia) or the "Mysterium Magnum," the spiritual matrix from which all creation originates.</note>, and we do as the Mother shows us; we know nothing of any other.

8. We are not born from the wisdom of this world, nor do we understand it; rather, what is given to us, that we give back. In this, we have no other created will, nor do we even know for what purpose we write, except what the Spirit shows us and which we set down for you. We work thus in our vineyard, in which the House-Father <note>A biblical reference to God as the master of the vineyard in the parables of Jesus.</note> has placed us, hoping also to enjoy the lovely grapes, which we often receive from the Paradise of God.

9. We wish to speak as if before many, and yet we feel we write it for ourselves, all of which is hidden in God. For the fiery impulse <note>original: "feurige Trieb." Böhme frequently describes his inspiration as an internal "fire" or spiritual heat that compels him to write thoughts he does not fully understand with his own intellect.</note> will have it so, as if we spoke from many and also before many, though of this I know nothing.

# Chapter 6: Of Man.

10. Therefore, should it happen that this is read, let no one consider it a work of external reason; rather, it has been produced out of the inner, hidden man. It is according to that inner man that this hand has written, without regard for any person’s status. 

11. We therefore exhort the reader that he would go into himself and behold himself in the inward man; if he does so, we shall be very sweet and dear to him. We say this without joking, in all faithfulness.

12. If we rightly recollect ourselves in this knowledge, we see clearly that we have been led as if imprisoned until now; and specifically by the clever ones of this world, who have kept us locked in their art of reason <term>Vernunft-Kunst: Böhme’s term for human logic and academic cleverness divorced from spiritual experience</term>, so that we have had to see through their eyes, both in Philosophy <note>original: "Philosophia"</note> and Theology <note>original: "Theologia"</note>. And this spirit, which has led us captive for so long, may rightly be called the Anti-Christ. I find no other name for it in the light of nature by which I could call it, other than the Anti-Christ in Babel <note>original: "Babel." For Böhme, this signifies the "city of confusion"—the corrupt institutional church and the vanity of worldly systems.</note>. Mark this diligently: you shall see him riding; he shall be shown to you clearly. You need no spectacles for this, nor any Academy. He rides over the whole world in all castles, cities, and villages; over body and soul. Therefore the angel in the Revelation <note>original: "Offenbarung"</note> bids us to go out from him. He is so proud that he rides over heaven and earth, yes, even over the Godhead. He is a king, riding over the <term>Principle</term> <note>original: "Principium." In Böhme’s terminology, a "Principle" refers to one of the three fundamental realms of existence: the dark fire-world, the light-world, or the outer world of nature.</note> of this world, and over hell.

13. Where will you ride then, you proud woman? <note>A reference to the Whore of Babylon from the Book of Revelation, symbolizing the corrupt worldly church.</note> When this <term>Principle</term> breaks, you will be outside of GOD with all the devils. Why do you not stay here with the children?

14. O Adam, if only you had not sat upon that proud beast! If only you had remained with the children of God in Paradise! How does it help you that you ride over God in a foreign Principle? Would it not be better for you to be in God? What use to you is the wisdom of the stars <note>original: "Wiße der Sternen." This refers to astrology and the study of the physical cosmos as a source of prideful "hidden" knowledge.</note>, that you ride in pride as if you were your own God? You ride only into death; who will lead you out if you do not dismount from your beast? There is no one, neither in heaven nor in this world, who can lead you out, except only a humble, simple, slaughtered Lamb, who does not carry the wisdom of this world. How will you come out, as long as you ride upon a dragon? The Lamb

### III. Of the Threefold Life, Chapter 6.

28. Thus we are all set against one another: We carry the name of Christ and are within His covenant; we have said "Yes," but those who do not act upon it are useless servants and live outside the Father's will. But if the Turks <note>original: "Türcken." In Böhme's time, this was a general term for Muslims. 29. Or do you think I am confirming their blindness, so that they should continue as they are? No, I am showing you *your* blindness—you who carry Christ’s name, you who judge others yet do the very same things you condemn, knowingly bringing God’s judgment upon yourself. He who said, *Love your enemies and do good to those who persecute you*, does not teach you to judge or revile, but rather the way of gentleness. You should be a light to the world, so that the heathens may see by your works that you are God’s children.

30. When we remember our true humanity, which is the right **likeness and image of God**, we find God within us, yet find ourselves to be outside of God. It now depends on this: that we enter back into ourselves, into God, into our hidden man.

31. If we then set our **will** with right and earnest simplicity in God, we depart from this world with Christ—leaving the stars and elements—and enter into God.

32. For in the will of **Reason**, we are children of the stars and elements, and the spirit of this world rules over us. But if we go out from the will of this world and into the will toward God, then the Spirit of God rules in us and confirms us as His children; also, the <term>paradisiacal wreath: "paradeisische Kränzlein," a mystical symbol in Böhme's work representing spiritual rebirth, virginity of the soul, and the restoration of the divine image</term> is placed upon the soul. Then the soul becomes as an "unknowing child" in this world, for she loses the master of this world <note>The "master of this world" refers to worldly intellect and the ego-driven spirit of the age.</note> who previously led her by means of Reason.

33. O Man, consider who guides and leads you! For *Eternity without end* is a long time; temporal honor and goods are but **dung** before God. It all falls into the grave with you and comes to nothing; but to be in God’s will is eternal wealth and honor. There, all worry ceases; our **Mother** <note>In Böhme’s theology, this "Mother" often refers to Divine Wisdom (Sophia) or the celestial nature that nurtures the reborn soul.</note> cares for us, in whose lap we live as children.

No, we speak livingly in our own knowledge—not through opinions from the mouths of others, but from our own. 37. A blind man who does not see the light of the world is regarded like a sleeper who dreams; for he hears indeed of the world’s beauty, but he does not recognize it. He knows it only from hearsay, and yet often thinks a thing is better or worse because he does not see it; he imagines it according to the story. But he who sees the light himself speaks of the truth, for he grasps the essence.

38. Thus I say: in the outer man we are all sleeping, lying in the cradle, and letting **Reason** rock us. We see with the eyes of the hypocrisy of our deceivers, who hang bells and trinkets before our cradle so that we only sleep and play with their tinkling, so that they may remain masters of the house.

39. O blind **Reason**! Rise up from the cradle; for you are a child of the Mother and an heir to the goods—furthermore, both the child and the master of the house. Why do you let your servants treat you this way?

40. Christ says: *I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will have the light of eternal life.* (John 8: 12). He does not direct us to the hypocrites, murderers, and quarrellers, but only to himself. In His light we shall see, according to the inward eyes; thus we see Him, for He is the Light. When we see Him, we walk in the Light.

44. The stars are from the Center of Nature <note>original: "Centro Naturæ." Here meaning the spiritual or celestial space from which they emerged.</note>; for in the eternal Center there is no number, but rather the Almightiness in its rising is without number. For that which allows itself to be counted and grasped is not eternal; it has a beginning and an end. Thus we recognize that man’s spirit and soul have no beginning or end, and cannot be counted: which we understand in the "stars" of our mind <note>original: "Gemüthes." The deep seat of the soul’s thoughts and desires.</note>, from which the senses proceed, which are without number. For from one sense, in time, more other senses may proceed than there are stars in the firmament; in this we recognize our eternity and rejoice greatly that we know such a thing.

45. Understand us correctly, as to how this world is in its foundation: the eternal Center of the birth of life and of essence is everywhere. If you enclose a small circle, even like a tiny grain, the entire birth of eternal nature is within it, and also the Trinity in the <term>Holy Ternary</term> <note>original: "Ternario Sancto." A term for the divine realm where the Trinity is revealed through spiritual substance.</note>. But you do not enclose the eternal nature, nor do you grasp it—much less the Trinity—rather, you grasp the offspring from the Center; the eternal nature is ungraspable, just as God is.

### Chapter 6. Of Man. 127
<meta>catchword: in</meta>

100. Christ says: *Seek, and you will find*, Matthew 7:7. He wishes to be sought; no lazy person finds Him. Even if such a person carries Him within himself, he does not recognize Him. But the one to whom He reveals Himself is the only one who has joy in Him. For there is no end to His <term>virtue</term> <note>original: "Tugend." In Böhme's writing, this signifies not just moral goodness, but the inherent "power," "potency," or "divine energy" of a substance.</note>; whoever possesses Him does not give Him away. And even if he were to give Him away, He is of no use to the lazy man, for he does not learn His virtue.

101. But the seeker finds the virtue with the **Stone**, so that when he finds it and recognizes that it is certain, there is greater joy in him than the world is capable of—joy that no pen can write, and no tongue can speak of in an <term>Adam-like way</term> <note>original: "auf Adamische Art." This refers to the fallen, earthly, and limited mode of human language and perception inherited from Adam.</note>.

102. To Adam-like eyes, this Stone is to be regarded as the most humble and plain of all stones; it is stepped upon with the feet, for it gives no luster to the eyes. If one trips over it, it is cast away as if it were useless; no one asks after it, and yet it is sought so intensely in the world. There is no person on earth who does not desire it; all the high and the wise seek it. They may well find one and imagine it is the right one, but they miss it. They try to add power and virtue to it, thinking they must maintain it once they have it, but that is not it; for it requires no added virtue—all virtues lie hidden within it.

103. The one who has it and knows it—as the one who seeks it—may find everything that is in heaven and earth; he finds that.

104. This is the **Stone** that is rejected by the builders, and it is a great **cornerstone**, Matthew 21:42, 44. Upon whomever it falls, it shall crush them and kindle a fire within them. All the high schools <note>A common term in this period for universities or academic institutions, which Böhme often criticized for their intellectual pride.</note> seek it, but with their seeking, they do not find it. Occasionally, one who seeks it rightly finds it; but the others despise him and cast him away, and so it remains hidden.

**2.** We need no hypocrites or ear-ticklers <note>Those who tell people only what they want to hear to gain favor.</note> who comfort us and promise us many mountains of gold, only so that we follow after them and make them shine.
